# Lummis Releases Updated Clarity Act Text Ahead of Historic Tuesday Vote

September 10, 2026

Washington, D.C.— U.S. Senate Banking Digital Assets Subcommittee Chair Cynthia Lummis (R-WY) released updated text for the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act as the Senate prepares to vote on the bill next Tuesday, September 15th. This text reflects the continued, bipartisan hard work accomplished over the August recess. 

Updates to the text include:

  * Provisions addressing when non-decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols must register with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and be subject to the Bank Secrecy Act, similar to provisions in section 10301 of the Banking devision of the Clarity Act. 
  * Specifying that DeFi provisions only apply to spot and cash digital commodity transactions, addressing tribal concerns about the potential impact of this legislation on prediction markets. 
  * Clarifications to the powers of credit unions to conduct digital asset activities.

“Nearly a decade ago, Wyoming wrote the blueprint for digital asset regulation, and this bill finally brings that clarity to the rest of the country,” said Lummis.

# Lummis, Boozman, Scott Release Final Clarity Act Text 

September 14, 2026

Washington, D.C.— U.S. Senate Banking Digital Assets Subcommittee Chair Cynthia Lummis (R-WY) alongside Chairmen John Boozman (R-AR) and Tim Scott (R-SC) released a final draft of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act before Tuesday’s vote, reflecting over a year of bipartisan negotiations and 126 substantive changes made at the request of Democrats. 

The final text includes new ethics language which reflects substantially all of the Tillis-Gallego ethics proposal, including a meaningful role for state attorneys general in enforcement. It also gives the Secretary of the Treasury new authority to prevent deposit flight tied to payment stablecoins, providing a strong circuit-breaker to protect community banks and the farmers and small businesses who rely on them. The draft also includes edits to the Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act (BRCA) to shield developers from money transmission registration requirements and establish a strong civil safe harbor.

# SENATOR MCCORMICK RELEASES STATEMENT ON THE CLARITY ACT

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, the Senate failed to advance the CLARITY Act after a procedural vote fell short of the 60 votes needed (49-50). Following the vote, Senator Dave McCormick (R-PA) released the following statement:

“Today, Senate Democrats blocked the vote to advance the CLARITY Act. I’m deeply disappointed at this outcome. For more than a year, Republicans and Democrats worked together in good faith to develop a clear, responsible regulatory framework for digital assets. The legislation before the Senate today incorporated substantive changes requested by Democrats, real concessions designed to address concerns from both sides of the aisle and build a durable bipartisan framework. The status quo leaves consumers and investors worse off and cedes U.S. financial leadership overseas. At a time when our global competitors are racing ahead, American entrepreneurs, investors, consumers, and financial institutions in Pennsylvania and across the U.S. deserve clear rules of the road that protect consumers while allowing innovation to flourish here at home. This issue isn’t going away, and neither is my commitment to getting it done. Community banks and entrepreneurs in Pennsylvania are worse off without CLARITY. I’ll continue working with colleagues on both sides of the aisle to deliver the certainty America needs to remain the global leader in financial innovation.”

# Warner Statement on CLARITY Act

WASHINGTON – U.S. Sen. Mark R. Warner (D-VA) released the following statement after voting against cloture on the CLARITY Act:

“I have long believed Congress needs to establish clear rules of the road for digital assets that protect consumers, safeguard our national security, and give responsible companies the certainty they need to operate in the United States.

“But we cannot pass landmark legislation governing this industry while allowing the President of the United States to personally profit from it. The president should not be able to use the power and influence of his office to benefit his own crypto holdings while his administration makes decisions that could directly affect their value. At a minimum, any serious crypto legislation must include meaningful ethics requirements that prevent the president and other senior government officials from profiting off the policies they oversee.

“I want to get to yes on responsible digital asset legislation, and no one has worked harder or spent more time engaging in good faith to try to get this done. We got close to resolving some of the toughest outstanding issues around law enforcement and national security, but ultimately, the failure to address this fundamental conflict of interest made it impossible for me to support moving forward. That is why I voted no today.”

Sec. 412. Other tradable assets 
Section 412 requires the trading of other types of tradable assets on or through a person registered 
with the CFTC to comply with the requirements of the Commodity Exchange Act as though the asset

Section 413 requires the CFTC to issue rules establishing requirements for the identification, 
mitigation, and resolution of conflicts of interest among entities and persons registered with the CFTC.  
 
Sec. 414. Effective date  
Section 414 provides that the provisions under this Title will take effect 270 days after the date of

# Lummis Releases Updated Clarity Act Text Ahead of Historic Tuesday Vote

September 10, 2026

Washington, D.C.— U.S. Senate Banking Digital Assets Subcommittee Chair Cynthia Lummis (R-WY) released updated text for the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act as the Senate prepares to vote on the bill next Tuesday, September 15th. This text reflects the continued, bipartisan hard work accomplished over the August recess. 

Updates to the text include:

  * Provisions addressing when non-decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols must register with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and be subject to the Bank Secrecy Act, similar to provisions in section 10301 of the Banking devision of the Clarity Act. 
  * Specifying that DeFi provisions only apply to spot and cash digital commodity transactions, addressing tribal concerns about the potential impact of this legislation on prediction markets. 
  * Clarifications to the powers of credit unions to conduct digital asset activities.

“Nearly a decade ago, Wyoming wrote the blueprint for digital asset regulation, and this bill finally brings that clarity to the rest of the country,” said Lummis.

# Lummis, Boozman, Scott Release Final Clarity Act Text 

September 14, 2026

Washington, D.C.— U.S. Senate Banking Digital Assets Subcommittee Chair Cynthia Lummis (R-WY) alongside Chairmen John Boozman (R-AR) and Tim Scott (R-SC) released a final draft of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act before Tuesday’s vote, reflecting over a year of bipartisan negotiations and 126 substantive changes made at the request of Democrats. 

The final text includes new ethics language which reflects substantially all of the Tillis-Gallego ethics proposal, including a meaningful role for state attorneys general in enforcement. It also gives the Secretary of the Treasury new authority to prevent deposit flight tied to payment stablecoins, providing a strong circuit-breaker to protect community banks and the farmers and small businesses who rely on them. The draft also includes edits to the Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act (BRCA) to shield developers from money transmission registration requirements and establish a strong civil safe harbor.

# SENATOR MCCORMICK RELEASES STATEMENT ON THE CLARITY ACT

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, the Senate failed to advance the CLARITY Act after a procedural vote fell short of the 60 votes needed (49-50). Following the vote, Senator Dave McCormick (R-PA) released the following statement:

“Today, Senate Democrats blocked the vote to advance the CLARITY Act. I’m deeply disappointed at this outcome. For more than a year, Republicans and Democrats worked together in good faith to develop a clear, responsible regulatory framework for digital assets. The legislation before the Senate today incorporated substantive changes requested by Democrats, real concessions designed to address concerns from both sides of the aisle and build a durable bipartisan framework. The status quo leaves consumers and investors worse off and cedes U.S. financial leadership overseas. At a time when our global competitors are racing ahead, American entrepreneurs, investors, consumers, and financial institutions in Pennsylvania and across the U.S. deserve clear rules of the road that protect consumers while allowing innovation to flourish here at home. This issue isn’t going away, and neither is my commitment to getting it done. Community banks and entrepreneurs in Pennsylvania are worse off without CLARITY. I’ll continue working with colleagues on both sides of the aisle to deliver the certainty America needs to remain the global leader in financial innovation.”

# Warner Statement on CLARITY Act

WASHINGTON – U.S. Sen. Mark R. Warner (D-VA) released the following statement after voting against cloture on the CLARITY Act:

“I have long believed Congress needs to establish clear rules of the road for digital assets that protect consumers, safeguard our national security, and give responsible companies the certainty they need to operate in the United States.

“But we cannot pass landmark legislation governing this industry while allowing the President of the United States to personally profit from it. The president should not be able to use the power and influence of his office to benefit his own crypto holdings while his administration makes decisions that could directly affect their value. At a minimum, any serious crypto legislation must include meaningful ethics requirements that prevent the president and other senior government officials from profiting off the policies they oversee.

“I want to get to yes on responsible digital asset legislation, and no one has worked harder or spent more time engaging in good faith to try to get this done. We got close to resolving some of the toughest outstanding issues around law enforcement and national security, but ultimately, the failure to address this fundamental conflict of interest made it impossible for me to support moving forward. That is why I voted no today.”

“This afternoon, Senate Democrats proved they were never truly serious about protecting consumers and preserving American leadership. I sat at the table with Senate Democrats working in good faith to get this done while they played games.
“For over a year, they presented demands and the second we met them, they made new demands and moved the goal posts. Today they voted against real limitations on politicians’ personal crypto investments. They voted against protecting American consumers from the scammers and fraudsters this bill would have shut down. They voted against American leadership, and handed China and every one of our foreign competitors exactly what they wanted. Democrats chose politics over the American people—again. That’s not leadership on their part, that’s surrender to their radical, socialist base.
“The once-proud Democratic party is anti-consumer and pro-illicit finance, anti-ethics, anti-free enterprise, anti-worker, anti-livable wage jobs, and pro-socialism. The Democrats are now anti-American. Sad!”

# Chairman Scott, Senate Banking Committee Advance Clarity Act in Historic Bipartisan Vote

Washington, D.C. — Chairman Tim Scott (R-S.C.) today led the Senate Banking Committee in a successful bipartisan markup to advance H.R. 3633, the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act of 2025, legislation to establish clear rules of the road for digital assets. After nearly a year of good-faith bipartisan negotiations, Senate Banking Committee Republicans and Democrats came together today to advance a comprehensive market structure bill that will establish America as the crypto capital of the world. The bill advanced out of committee today by a vote of 15-9 and now moves to the Senate floor.
“Today, the Banking Committee showed the American people that Washington can still work together. We had a serious debate, worked through real differences, and came together around a shared goal: protecting consumers, supporting innovation, and keeping the future of finance in America. This legislation brings digital assets into the sunlight with clear rules, stronger safeguards, and better tools to stop bad actors. For me, this is personal. My mother raised my brother and me with faith, grit, and determination, and she taught me that the American Dream should be within reach for every family, including single mothers working hard to build a better life for their children. Today is a historic day for this Committee and a major victory for the American people,” said Chairman Scott.

A "blockchain control person" is defined as any individual or group

Sec. 412. Other tradable assets 
Section 412 requires the trading of other types of tradable assets on or through a person registered 
with the CFTC to comply with the requirements of the Commodity Exchange Act as though the asset 
was a digital commodity. A tradable asset is defined as a digital asset which is not a digital commodity 
or other blockchain-based regulated financial product. The CFTC is permitted to impose additional 
requirements to address risks not captured by the existing regulatory regime. The section prohibits 
the listing of a digital commodity or tradable asset if its primary purpose is to commit fraud or market 
manipulation, further a scheme found in a final action by a competent court to be in violation of 
campaign finance or government ethics laws, or engage in any other conduct that would result in 
abusive practices or be disruptive to market integrity.   
 
Sec. 413. Conflict of interest rulemaking 
Section 413 requires the CFTC to issue rules establishing requirements for the identification, 
mitigation, and resolution of conflicts of interest among entities and persons registered with the CFTC.  
 
Sec. 414. Effective date  
Section 414 provides that the provisions under this Title will take effect 270 days after the date of 
enactment of the Act.  
 
Sec. 415. Sense of Congress  
Section 415 articulates the sense of Congress that nothing in this Act or any amendment made by this 
Act should be interpreted to authorize any entity to regulate any commodity, other than a digital 
commodity on any spot market.

L77: from intermediaries filing under the provisional registration would sunset after four years.

L1: Crypto Legislation: CLARITY Act’s (H.R. 3633)
L2: Potential Effects on SEC Jurisdiction
L3: July 10, 2025
L4: The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act of 2025 (CLARITY, H.R. 3633) passed the House Committees on
L5: Financial Services and Agriculture on June 10, 2025. The bill aims to transform digital asset regulatory
L6: landscape and redefine the regulatory roles at the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the
L7: Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). This Insight focuses on discussions of the SEC’s
L8: jurisdiction. For an overview of CLARITY, see CRS Insight IN12583, Crypto Legislation: An Overview
L9: of H.R. 3633, the CLARITY Act, by Paul Tierno.
L10: SEC’s Existing Regulatory Framework
L11: The SEC is the primary regulator overseeing digital and traditional security offerings, trading, and
L12: investment activities. The current regulatory framework at the SEC is technology neutral, meaning
L13: securities regulation generally applies to all securities whether they are digital or traditional. The SEC’s
L14: regulatory framework generally aligns with its mission to protect investors; maintain fair, orderly, and
L15: efficient markets; and facilitate capital formation. For more details, see CRS Report R48521, Capital
L16: Markets and Securities Regulation: Overview and Policy Issues, by Eva Su.
L17: For digital assets that are securities, the SEC has both (1) regulatory authority, including over digital asset
L18: securities, which include registration requirements, disclosure requirements, and market oversight; and (2)
L19: enforcement authority that allows it to bring civil enforcement actions, such as anti-fraud and anti-
L20: manipulation actions, for securities laws violations.
L21: SEC Chair Paul S. Atkins stated that the agency plans to develop new regulatory approaches for digital
L22: assets. The SEC’s Crypto Task Force, formed in January 2025, is leading this effort.
L23: Legislative Context
L24: Not all digital assets are legally classified as securities, and thus they may not fall under the securities
L25: regulation regime. Digital assets may also be commodities under the Commodity Exchange Act (P.L. 74-
L26: 675). In such cases, they are subject to the jurisdiction of the CFTC, which generally extends to

L37: instrument is a security-based derivative, both the SEC and the CFTC may have jurisdiction over it.
L38: No federal agency currently has general regulatory authority over spot transactions in digital assets (i.e.,
L39: assets that are bought and sold for immediate settlement, meaning the transactions are settled “on the
L40: spot”) that are not securities. As such, these markets do not feature the same rules and regulations as seen

L43: body—published a report that highlights the perceived “regulatory gap,” encouraging Congress to pass

L45: assets that are not securities. Some policymakers and legislators appear to be using this FSOC-described

L48: Potential Effects of CLARITY on SEC Jurisdiction
L49: CLARITY would generally grant the CFTC jurisdiction over digital assets that meet its definition of
L50: digital commodity and would narrow the SEC’s jurisdiction over digital asset securities. The SEC’s role
L51: would be reduced in several areas, including the following:
L52: •
L53: The bill acknowledges the view that a digital asset originally sold as part of an
L54: investment contract may, over time, become sufficiently decentralized or functionally
L55: “mature” such that it no longer meets the definition of security. To account for this, the
L56: bill would allow the issuer to file a notice with the SEC stating that the asset either is
L57: already mature or is expected to become so within four years. The SEC would review and
L58: decide whether to object. The bill would also direct the SEC to promulgate rules
L59: regarding consequences or penalties for failing to meet the promised maturity timeline.
L60: This approach differs from current securities regulation, where all digital asset
L61: securities—including those that are in the transition stage to become commodities—are
L62: subject to securities regulation.
L63: •
L64: The bill would create a new exemption from the Securities Act of 1933 for certain digital
L65: commodities issuers that offer and sell up to $75 million in assets within a 12-month
L66: period when certain disclosure and eligibility conditions are met. This exemption would
L67: require issuers to file initial and ongoing disclosures. Disclosure items would include
L68: maturity status, source code, token economics, and risk factors. The SEC would have one
L69: year from the bill’s enactment to promulgate rules governing the new exemption. Aspects
L70: of the exemption are similar to certain existing SEC private securities exemptions. For
L71: example, the SEC Regulation A Tier 2 offering (also known as Regulation A+) allows
L72: securities offerings of up to $75 million in a 12-month period. Issuers raising money
L73: through Regulation A+ face eligibility requirements, a scaled-down version of the
L74: disclosure requirement relative to public securities offerings, and bad actor
L75: disqualifications, among other requirements.
L76: •
L77: The bill would clarify that “permitted payment stablecoins” that meet the bill’s reserve
L78: and operational requirements would be generally excluded from securities regulation. But
L79: the SEC would retain certain anti-fraud and anti-manipulation authorities over them. This
L80: clarification would remove the possibility of generally applying securities regulation to
L81: applicable stablecoins. For example, it would eliminate uncertainty over whether
L82: stablecoins’ investment fund-like structures (e.g., structures mimicking money market

L7: The CLARITY Act establishes clear, functional requirements for digital asset market participants,
L8: prioritizing consumer protection while fostering innovation. By providing strong safeguards and long-

L10: America’s leadership in the global ﬁnancial system.

L13: •
L14: Digital assets and related blockchain technology have the potential to form the
L15: foundation of the next generation of ﬁnancial innovation.
L16: •
L17: However, regulation-by-enforcement and ongoing regulatory ambiguity have stiﬂed this
L18: innovative potential while leaving consumers unprotected.
L19: •
L20: The CLARITY Act addresses these challenges by establishing a clear regulatory
L21: framework for digital asset markets and closing the current regulatory gaps.
L22: •
L23: The CLARITY Act is essential to restoring conﬁdence in America’s regulatory
L24: environment, encouraging innovation, and keeping digital asset businesses in the U.S.
L25: The CLARITY Act will strengthen the market by fostering the development of digital asset
L26: projects:

L28: Digital asset developers will have a clear pathway to raise funds under the Securities

L33: Commission (CFTC).

L36: •
L37: The CLARITY Act establishes clear lines between the SEC and CFTC.
L38: •
L39: The CLARITY Act creates comprehensive registration regimes to permit digital asset
L40: ﬁrms to lawfully serve customers in digital asset markets.

L43: market participants:

L46: including information relating to the digital asset project’s operation, ownership, and
L47: structure.

L51: o Segregate customer funds from their own; and

L1: Crypto Legislation: CLARITY Act’s (H.R. 3633)
L2: Potential Effects on SEC Jurisdiction
L3: July 10, 2025
L4: The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act of 2025 (CLARITY, H.R. 3633) passed the House Committees on
L5: Financial Services and Agriculture on June 10, 2025. The bill aims to transform digital asset regulatory
L6: landscape and redefine the regulatory roles at the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the
L7: Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). This Insight focuses on discussions of the SEC’s
L8: jurisdiction. For an overview of CLARITY, see CRS Insight IN12583, Crypto Legislation: An Overview
L9: of H.R. 3633, the CLARITY Act, by Paul Tierno.
L10: SEC’s Existing Regulatory Framework
L11: The SEC is the primary regulator overseeing digital and traditional security offerings, trading, and
L12: investment activities. The current regulatory framework at the SEC is technology neutral, meaning
L13: securities regulation generally applies to all securities whether they are digital or traditional. The SEC’s
L14: regulatory framework generally aligns with its mission to protect investors; maintain fair, orderly, and
L15: efficient markets; and facilitate capital formation. For more details, see CRS Report R48521, Capital
L16: Markets and Securities Regulation: Overview and Policy Issues, by Eva Su.
L17: For digital assets that are securities, the SEC has both (1) regulatory authority, including over digital asset
L18: securities, which include registration requirements, disclosure requirements, and market oversight; and (2)
L19: enforcement authority that allows it to bring civil enforcement actions, such as anti-fraud and anti-
L20: manipulation actions, for securities laws violations.
L21: SEC Chair Paul S. Atkins stated that the agency plans to develop new regulatory approaches for digital
L22: assets. The SEC’s Crypto Task Force, formed in January 2025, is leading this effort.
L23: Legislative Context
L24: Not all digital assets are legally classified as securities, and thus they may not fall under the securities
L25: regulation regime. Digital assets may also be commodities under the Commodity Exchange Act (P.L. 74-
L26: 675). In such cases, they are subject to the jurisdiction of the CFTC, which generally extends to

L36: commodities and derivatives. While the CFTC does not regulate digital asset securities, if a digital asset
L37: instrument is a security-based derivative, both the SEC and the CFTC may have jurisdiction over it.
L38: No federal agency currently has general regulatory authority over spot transactions in digital assets (i.e.,
L39: assets that are bought and sold for immediate settlement, meaning the transactions are settled “on the
L40: spot”) that are not securities. As such, these markets do not feature the same rules and regulations as seen
L41: within the securities regulatory framework to safeguard investors, deter market manipulation, and ensure
L42: efficient market operations. The Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC)—a systemic risk oversight
L43: body—published a report that highlights the perceived “regulatory gap,” encouraging Congress to pass
L44: legislation that provides regulatory authority for federal financial regulators over spot markets for digital
L45: assets that are not securities. Some policymakers and legislators appear to be using this FSOC-described
L46: regulatory gap as a rationale for the crypto legislative proposals to reform the digital asset market
L47: structure.
L48: Potential Effects of CLARITY on SEC Jurisdiction
L49: CLARITY would generally grant the CFTC jurisdiction over digital assets that meet its definition of
L50: digital commodity and would narrow the SEC’s jurisdiction over digital asset securities. The SEC’s role
L51: would be reduced in several areas, including the following:
L52: •
L53: The bill acknowledges the view that a digital asset originally sold as part of an
L54: investment contract may, over time, become sufficiently decentralized or functionally
L55: “mature” such that it no longer meets the definition of security. To account for this, the
L56: bill would allow the issuer to file a notice with the SEC stating that the asset either is
L57: already mature or is expected to become so within four years. The SEC would review and
L58: decide whether to object. The bill would also direct the SEC to promulgate rules
L59: regarding consequences or penalties for failing to meet the promised maturity timeline.
L60: This approach differs from current securities regulation, where all digital asset
L61: securities—including those that are in the transition stage to become commodities—are
L62: subject to securities regulation.
L63: •
L64: The bill would create a new exemption from the Securities Act of 1933 for certain digital
L65: commodities issuers that offer and sell up to $75 million in assets within a 12-month
L66: period when certain disclosure and eligibility conditions are met. This exemption would
L67: require issuers to file initial and ongoing disclosures. Disclosure items would include
L68: maturity status, source code, token economics, and risk factors. The SEC would have one
L69: year from the bill’s enactment to promulgate rules governing the new exemption. Aspects
L70: of the exemption are similar to certain existing SEC private securities exemptions. For
L71: example, the SEC Regulation A Tier 2 offering (also known as Regulation A+) allows
L72: securities offerings of up to $75 million in a 12-month period. Issuers raising money
L73: through Regulation A+ face eligibility requirements, a scaled-down version of the
L74: disclosure requirement relative to public securities offerings, and bad actor
L75: disqualifications, among other requirements.
L76: •
L77: The bill would clarify that “permitted payment stablecoins” that meet the bill’s reserve
L78: and operational requirements would be generally excluded from securities regulation. But
L79: the SEC would retain certain anti-fraud and anti-manipulation authorities over them. This
L80: clarification would remove the possibility of generally applying securities regulation to
L81: applicable stablecoins. For example, it would eliminate uncertainty over whether
L82: stablecoins’ investment fund-like structures (e.g., structures mimicking money market
L83: mutual funds and exchange-traded funds) could trigger securities regulation. Draft

L0: The Digital Asset Market Clarity (CLARITY) Act
L1: 
L2: The CLARITY Act, sponsored by House Committee on Financial Services Chairman French Hill (AR-02)
L3: and House Committee on Agriculture Chairman G.T. Thompson (PA-15) was introduced on May 29,
L4: 2025, and has 20 cosponsors (13 Republicans, 7 Democrats). The bill advanced out of both
L5: Committees with bipartisan support on June 10, 2025.
L6: 
L7: The CLARITY Act establishes clear, functional requirements for digital asset market participants,
L8: prioritizing consumer protection while fostering innovation. By providing strong safeguards and long-
L9: overdue regulatory certainty, this bipartisan legislation advances American innovation and reinforces
L10: America’s leadership in the global ﬁnancial system.
L11: 
L12: Why is the CLARITY Act needed?
L13: •
L14: Digital assets and related blockchain technology have the potential to form the
L15: foundation of the next generation of ﬁnancial innovation.
L16: •
L17: However, regulation-by-enforcement and ongoing regulatory ambiguity have stiﬂed this
L18: innovative potential while leaving consumers unprotected.
L19: •
L20: The CLARITY Act addresses these challenges by establishing a clear regulatory
L21: framework for digital asset markets and closing the current regulatory gaps.
L22: •
L23: The CLARITY Act is essential to restoring conﬁdence in America’s regulatory
L24: environment, encouraging innovation, and keeping digital asset businesses in the U.S.
L25: The CLARITY Act will strengthen the market by fostering the development of digital asset
L26: projects:
L27: •
L28: Digital asset developers will have a clear pathway to raise funds under the Securities
L29: and Exchange Commission’s (SEC) jurisdiction.
L30: •
L31: Market participants will have a trusted pathway to trade digital commodities through
L32: intermediaries and exchanges overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading
L33: Commission (CFTC).
L34: 
L35: The CLARITY Act will provide certainty to customer-facing digital asset ﬁrms:
L36: •
L37: The CLARITY Act establishes clear lines between the SEC and CFTC.
L38: •
L39: The CLARITY Act creates comprehensive registration regimes to permit digital asset
L40: ﬁrms to lawfully serve customers in digital asset markets.
L41: 
L42: The CLARITY Act will protect consumers by strengthening transparency and accountability for
L43: market participants:
L44: •
L45: Digital asset developers will be required to provide accurate, relevant disclosures,
L46: including information relating to the digital asset project’s operation, ownership, and
L47: structure.
L48: •
L49: Customer-facing digital asset ﬁrms will be required to:
L50: o Provide appropriate disclosures to customers;
L51: o Segregate customer funds from their own; and
L52: o Address conﬂicts of interest through registration, disclosure, and operational
L53: requirements.

**CLARITY Act**는 미국의 가상자산 규제 체계를 정비하려는 법안으로, 정식 명칭은 **Digital Asset Market Clarity Act of 2025(H.R. 3633)**입니다.

핵심은 “어떤 가상자산을 누가 감독할 것인가”를 명확히 하는 것입니다.

- **디지털 상품(digital commodity)**과 현물시장은 주로 **CFTC(상품선물거래위원회)**가 감독
- 증권 성격의 토큰 발행·투자계약은 계속 **SEC(증권거래위원회)**가 감독
- 특정 블록체인이 충분히 탈중앙화된 **‘성숙한 블록체인’**이 되면, 관련 토큰이 증권 규제에서 디지털 상품 규제로 이동할 수 있는 절차 마련
- 거래소·브로커·딜러에 CFTC 등록 의무를 부과하고 고객자산 분리보관, 공시, 장부관리, 이해상충 방지, 자금세탁방지 등의 규칙 적용
- 일정 조건을 갖춘 프로젝트에는 12개월간 최대 7,500만 달러 규모의 토큰 판매에 제한적 SEC 등록 면제를 제공
- 스테이블코인은 대체로 별도 규제체계 대상으로 취급

쉽게 말하면, 현재의 “이 코인은 증권인가 상품인가?”라는 불확실성을 줄이고, 미국 가상자산 현물시장에도 거래소 등록과 고객보호 규칙을 만들자는 법안입니다. 다만 모든 코인을 자동으로 상품으로 인정하는 법안은 아닙니다. 블록체인의 통제 구조, 토큰 판매 방식, 공시 요건 등에 따라 판단하도록 설계됐습니다. [미 의회조사국(CRS) 법안 개요](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IN/PDF/IN12583/IN12583.1.pdf)

찬성 측은 규제 불확실성을 줄이고 소비자 보호와 미국 내 산업 성장을 동시에 달성할 수 있다고 봅니다. 반대·우려 측은 SEC 권한이 지나치게 축소될 수 있고, 발행사가 ‘탈중앙화’를 내세워 증권법을 회피할 가능성이나 CFTC의 감독 인력·예산 부족을 지적합니다. [CRS의 SEC 관할 분석](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IN/PDF/IN12584/IN12584.1.pdf)

**현재 상태(2026년 11월 18일 기준): 아직 법률은 아닙니다.** 하원에서는 2025년 7월 17일 **294대 134로 통과**됐고, 상원 위원회도 수정안을 진전시켰지만, 2026년 9월 15일 상원 본회의 심의를 진행하기 위한 종결투표가 필요한 60표를 얻지 못해 **49대 50으로 부결**됐습니다. 따라서 현재는 상원에서 사실상 멈춰 있으며, 재협상이나 새 법안 추진이 필요합니다. [하원 금융서비스위원회](https://financialservices.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?documentid=410815), [상원 은행위원회](https://www.banking.senate.gov/newsroom/majority/scott-statement-on-clarity-act-vote)

참고로 **GENIUS Act가 스테이블코인 발행자를 중심으로 규율하는 법**이라면, CLARITY Act는 가상자산의 분류와 거래시장 전반을 다루는 **시장구조 법안**이라는 차이가 있습니다.
